nameStory: Northern Shrimp gets its straightforward name from living in the cold northern waters of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. It's also called 'pink shrimp' for its delicate rosy color, and 'Maine shrimp' because it's been an important fishery species along Maine's coast for generations.
description: Northern Shrimp is a small, translucent crustacean that lives in the deep, cold waters off New England's coast. These delicate creatures have a curved, compressed body that's typically pinkish or pale orange in color. They're part of the decapod group, meaning they have ten legs like lobsters and crabs, but with a much more slender, graceful build. Adults usually measure 3-5 inches long from head to tail.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Curved, laterally compressed body that feels smooth and slightly firm when fresh, with a distinctive hump-backed appearance

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Translucent pink to pale orange body with darker reddish spots, often with a pearlescent sheen that catches light

idTips.label: Rostrum
idTips.description: Long, pointed beak-like projection from the head with small teeth along the top edge that feels sharp to the touch

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, dark compound eyes that bulge prominently from the head on short stalks

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, thread-like antennae that are often longer than the body and feel delicate and flexible

idTips.label: Swimming Legs
idTips.description: Five pairs of small, feathery swimming appendages under the curved abdomen that feel soft and brush-like

habitat: Northern Shrimp live in deep, cold waters along New England's continental shelf, typically 150-1500 feet deep where temperatures stay between 35-45°F year-round. They prefer muddy or sandy bottoms and are most commonly found in the Gulf of Maine. You're most likely to encounter them in fish markets, restaurants, or occasionally washed up on beaches after storms.

seasonality.spring: Peak fishing season begins as shrimp move into shallower waters. Look for them in fish markets and coastal restaurants during this time.
seasonality.summer: Less commonly available as they move to deeper, cooler waters. Occasionally found in deeper tide pools after strong storms.
seasonality.fall: Begin moving back toward shore in preparation for winter breeding season. Fresh catches may appear in local markets again.
seasonality.winter: Traditional harvesting season when they're closer to shore for breeding. Most likely time to find fresh local specimens in New England markets.

funFact: Northern Shrimp are all born male and then change into females as they get older and larger - a process called sequential hermaphroditism that helps ensure the biggest, strongest individuals become the egg-carrying mothers!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small shrimp in markets, but Northern Shrimp have a distinctly more curved, hump-backed body compared to straighter warm-water shrimp varieties. Remember: 'Northern curves, southern straight' - cold-water shrimp have more pronounced body curves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'shrimp' in America, many other countries call these 'prawns' - there's no scientific difference between the terms, just regional preference. The Food and Agriculture Organization officially calls them 'northern prawns,' which often confuses New Englanders used to the 'shrimp' name.
compareHints: Northern Shrimp can be distinguished from their close relative, the Aesop Shrimp, by their larger size and more pronounced body curve. Northern Shrimp also tend to have a more uniform pink coloration, while Aesop Shrimp often show more distinct banding patterns. The rostrum (beak) on Northern Shrimp is typically longer and more prominently toothed than on Aesop Shrimp.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Northern shrimp, the Aesop shrimp is distinguished by its pronounced curved back profile and slightly more robust build.
